a: to confirm and renew the friendship with the Romans
p: Judas had first made a treaty with Rome; Jonathan renews it about 144 BC.
b: Judas sent envoys to Rome in 161 BC, and the Senate made a treaty of friendship and alliance with the Jews (8:17–32). Treaties with Rome were personal: when a ruler died or a new one rose, the friendship was renewed. Jonathan, now high priest and the strongest man in the region (11:57–59), sends envoys about 144 BC. Josephus retells the embassy and says the Romans gave the envoys letters for safe passage (Antiquities 13.163–165). Rome promised little in practice, but a Roman tie gave the Jews standing with the quarrelling Seleucid kings.

p: Sparta was famous but no longer powerful. The link mattered for prestige and for an old claim of kinship.
b: By the 140s BC Sparta was a small city whose great days were long past; Rome had just crushed the Greek leagues (146 BC). So the letter is not about soldiers. A tie with the most famous city of old Greece gave the Jews a place among the respected peoples of the Greek world, against those who mocked them as a new and lawless people. The kinship claim (12:21) was already known: the high priest Jason fled to the Spartans "because of their kinship" in 168 BC (2 Maccabees 5:9). The KJV calls them by their older name, "the Lacedemonians".

p: The envoys go before the Roman Senate, which then handled foreign treaties.
b: The Greek bouleutērion means a council chamber, and 8:15 renders it so; here "the Senate house" names the Roman one. In Rome the Senate received foreign envoys and voted on treaties, which the consuls then carried out. 1 Maccabees 8:15 has already described the Senate as 320 men who meet every day. The letter of 15:16–21 shows what such a vote looked like in practice: a consul wrote to the kings and cities in Rome's sphere.

p: The high priest writes with the council of elders, the priests and the people: Judea speaks as a self-governing nation.
b: The heading copies the form of Greek city letters, where "the council and the people" write together. Here the high priest comes first, then the gerousia (the council of elders, the body that later became the Sanhedrin), then the priests and the people (dēmos). The same four groups receive the Spartans' reply to Simon (14:20). They show how the book wants Judea seen: a nation with its own leaders, not a Seleucid district.

p: Areus I ruled Sparta from 309 to 265 BC, so the Onias meant is probably Onias I, about 300 BC.
b: Sparta had two kings named Areus. Areus I reigned from 309 to 265 BC; Areus II died as a boy about 254 BC. Four high priests named Onias are known. Only Onias I (about 300 BC) lived at the time of Areus I, so most historians take the letter as written to him. Josephus gives the letter in different words and attaches it to a later Onias (Antiquities 12.225–227), which does not fit the Spartan dates. On whether the letter is genuine, see 12:21.

a: the holy books in our hands
p: One of the earliest names for a collection of Scripture: Jonathan trusts the holy books more than treaties.
b: "The holy books" (ta biblia ta hagia) is one of the oldest phrases for a body of sacred writings. The prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC) speaks of "the law, the prophets and the other books", and 2 Maccabees 2:13–15 says Judas gathered the books scattered by the war. Which books 1 Maccabees means is not said: certainly the law and the prophets, and probably the Psalms. The sentence also states the book's view of alliances: the Jews do not need Sparta, because their encouragement comes from Scripture and from "the help from Heaven" (12:15). Yet they keep the friendship up, so faith and diplomacy sit side by side.
orig: τὰ βιβλία τὰ ἅγια (ta biblia ta hagia)

a: in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers
p: The Temple remembers the Spartans in its sacrifices and prayers, as it later prayed for Persian and Roman rulers.
b: Praying for foreign rulers and friends at the Temple had a long history. Darius asked the Jews to "pray for the life of the king and of his sons" (Ezra 6:10), Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7), and in Roman times a daily sacrifice was offered for the emperor until it was stopped at the start of the war with Rome in AD 66 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.409). The claim here that the Spartans are remembered "without fail" is a diplomatic courtesy, but it rests on that real practice.

p: "Heaven" here stands for God, whom 1 Maccabees almost never names.
b: The Greek says simply "the help from heaven" (ek ouranōn). 1 Maccabees, in the text printed here, never names God as "God" or "Lord" at all, in narration or in speeches; it speaks of "Heaven" instead (3:18–19, 50, 60; 4:10, 24, 40, 55; 9:46; 16:3). The habit of saying "Heaven" for God shows up in Daniel 4:26 ("Heaven rules") and later in the rabbis' "the fear of Heaven" and Matthew's "kingdom of heaven". The Plain gives it a capital letter when it means God.
orig: τὴν ἐξ οὐρανῶν βοηθίαν (tēn ex ouranōn boēthian)

a: Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason
p: Both envoys carry Greek names, and so do their fathers: the Hasmonean court was at home in the Greek world.
b: Numenius and Antipater have Greek names, and their fathers are named Antiochus and Jason. Antiochus was the name of the king the book blames for the crisis of 175–164 BC (1:10), and Jason that of the high priest whom 2 Maccabees blames (2 Maccabees 4:7–10). Yet these families served the Hasmoneans loyally. Jewish families had used Greek names for generations, and the Hasmonean state, for all its zeal for the law, needed men who spoke Greek and knew Greek diplomacy. Antipater son of Jason may be the son of the Jason son of Eleazar whom Judas sent to Rome (8:17). Numenius goes again in 14:24 and returns in 15:15.

t: Were the Spartans kin to the Jews?
p: Areus says Spartans and Jews both descend from Abraham. Many historians doubt the letter.
b: The claim surprises modern readers, but Greek cities often found or invented ancient kinship with peoples they wanted as friends, usually through a hero's travels. Some Jewish writers of the time linked Abraham's sons by Keturah with distant nations (Genesis 25:1–4; Josephus, Antiquities 1.239–241, quoting Cleodemus Malchus on Africa). Is the letter genuine? Its Greek, as we have it, has passed through Hebrew and back, so its wording proves little. Some scholars accept a real exchange of courtesies, perhaps about 300 BC; many think it was composed later, in Judea, to give the treaty of 12:6–18 a past. Erich Gruen argued that the idea of kinship was a Jewish invention meant to place Israel among the honored peoples of the Greek world. Sparta's reply to Simon (14:20–23) is more widely accepted as authentic.

a: It has turned up in a document
p: The Greek εὑρέθη ἐν γραφῇ, "it was found in a writing", does not say what writing.
b: Areus says the kinship "was found in a writing" (heurethē en graphē), the usual phrase for something discovered in archives or old books. It does not claim a sacred text. Codex Alexandrinus spells it ἐγγενοῦς, a common way of writing ἐκ γένους in manuscripts and papyri; Swete's text prints ἐκ γένους, and the sense is the same.

a: your herds and your possessions are ours, and ours are yours
p: A formula of close alliance, like Jehoshaphat's "I am as you are".
b: The phrase is a way of pledging full friendship, not a promise to share property. Israel's kings used the same kind of words: Jehoshaphat told Ahab, "I am one with you, my people one with your people, my horses one with your horses" (1 Kings 22:4). Whether a Spartan king would write this way is one reason some scholars think the letter took its shape in Hebrew.

p: The kingdom is split: Demetrius II against Tryphon, who rules for the boy Antiochus VI.
b: Since 145 BC the Seleucid throne had two claimants. Demetrius II held part of the kingdom; his general Tryphon had set up Alexander Balas's young son as Antiochus VI (11:39–40, 54–56). Jonathan had backed Antiochus VI and fought for him (11:57–74). Demetrius's commanders now come back after their defeat at Hazor (11:63–74). The rivalry gave the Jews room to win more freedom, since each side bid for their help.

p: Jonathan meets the enemy far north, in the region of Hamath on the Orontes, in central Syria.
b: Hamath (modern Hama in Syria) lay on the Orontes River, at the northern edge of the land promised to Israel ("Lebo-hamath", Numbers 34:8). Fighting so far north was a new thing for a Jewish army. The book's comment that Jonathan "gave them no chance to set foot in his own country" explains why: he takes the war to the enemy. The Eleutherus River (12:30, the modern Nahr al-Kabir) was the boundary between the Seleucid and the old Ptolemaic lands.

a: they lit fires in their camp
p: The enemy lit fires so the Jews would think the camp was still full while they slipped away.
b: Leaving fires burning in an empty camp was an old trick for a night retreat, and Greek writers on warfare describe it. Jonathan's scouts see the fires (12:29) and think the enemy are still there. The Greek says the enemy "shrank in heart" (eptēxan tēn kardian), a vivid word for cowering. Jonathan's whole-night watch (12:27) won the battle without a fight.

p: An Arab tribe of the Anti-Lebanon region, near the town still called Zabadani, northwest of Damascus.
b: The name probably survives in Zabadani, a town in the Anti-Lebanon mountains northwest of Damascus. Jonathan, having missed the Seleucid army, strikes its Arab allies instead and then marches through the Damascus region. Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus spell the name Zabadeous (Swete's note).

t: Joppa, Judea's door to the sea
p: Simon seizes Joppa, the port Judea had long wanted, before it can be handed to Demetrius.
b: Joppa (Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv) was the only good harbor on the coast near Judea. Jonathan had taken it in 147 BC (10:75–76). Now Simon occupies it to keep its non-Jewish citizens from handing it to Demetrius, and later he drives them out and settles Jews there (13:11; 14:5, 34). Holding Joppa gave Judea trade and an outlet to "the islands of the sea" (14:5). Antiochus VII later demands it back (15:28–35). In the Hebrew Bible Joppa is where Jonah took ship (Jonah 1:3) and where cedar for the Temple was floated in (2 Chronicles 2:16).

a: to raise a great rampart between the Citadel and the city
p: Jonathan starves the Seleucid garrison in the Citadel by cutting it off from the city's markets.
b: The Citadel (the Akra) was the fortress the Seleucids built in Jerusalem in 167 BC, held by a garrison and by Jews who had taken the king's side (1:33–36). It stood close to the Temple, and from it they "used to go out and defile the area around the sanctuary" (14:36). Jonathan's wall cuts it off from the city's food and trade, and the plan works: in 141 BC hunger forces the garrison out (13:49–50). Where the Citadel stood is still debated: south of the Temple mount on the old City of David ridge is the most common view, and a wall and towers found in the Givati excavations (2015) have been proposed as part of it.

p: A section of Jerusalem's wall, otherwise unknown; the name may be Aramaic.
b: No other source names this part of the wall. Some connect the name with Aramaic words for "hunger" or a "double" wall, but no explanation is sure. The Vulgate calls it Caphetetha (Vulgate 12:37). The ravine on the east is the Kidron valley. Sinaiticus adds that they gathered "to build the city", which the KJV follows ("to build up the city"); Venetus has "cities".

p: A town in the low hills west of Judea, guarding the road from the coast to Jerusalem.
b: Adida is probably biblical Hadid (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 11:34), near modern Lod. The Shephelah is the band of low hills between the coastal plain and the Judean hill country. Simon's fortress there blocks the main road from the coast, and he camps there to face Tryphon (13:13). Sinaiticus and Venetus add "and set up" (gates), which only spells out what fortifying meant.

a: Tryphon wanted to become king of Asia
p: Tryphon, a general, had set up the boy Antiochus VI as a puppet king. Now he wants the crown for himself.
b: Diodotus, called Tryphon ("the Magnificent"), was a general from Apamea. In 145 BC he put Antiochus VI, the young son of Alexander Balas, on the throne against Demetrius II (11:39–40, 54). "King of Asia" was the Seleucid kings' own claim (8:6; 11:13). Jonathan was Antiochus VI's ally and confirmed in office by him (11:57), so he stood in the way. Tryphon killed the boy king about 142 BC (13:31–32) and ruled until Antiochus VII defeated him (15:10–14, 37).

p: The Greek "Bethsa" is Beth-shan, the old fortress town at the east end of the Jezreel valley.
b: Alexandrinus spells it Βεθσά, Sinaiticus and Venetus Βαιθσαν. It is Beth-shan (Joshua 17:11; 1 Samuel 31:10), called Scythopolis in Greek times (2 Maccabees 12:29–30), today Beit She'an. It controlled the road from the Jordan valley into Galilee and the coast, so it was a natural place for the two armies to meet.

a: introduced him to all his Friends
p: Tryphon gives Jonathan every public honor, the usual courtesies of the Greek courts, to lure him in.
b: Receiving a man "with honor", introducing him to one's "friends" (the courtiers) and giving gifts were the marks of royal favor; Jonathan had received the same from Alexander Balas and Demetrius (10:59–65; 11:26–27). Tryphon's flattery hides a trap. The narrator does not blame Jonathan openly, but his trust (12:46, "Jonathan trusted him") is the hinge of the story. The book's readers knew the warning of Psalm 146:3: "Do not rely on nobles."

a: That is why I am here
p: Tryphon promises to give Jonathan Ptolemais, the great harbor city of Acco, which Jews had long wanted.
b: Ptolemais is ancient Acco (Judges 1:31), renamed by the Ptolemies. It was the main port of the north and a Seleucid stronghold, hostile to the Jews (5:15, 22; 12:48). Demetrius I had offered it to the sanctuary (10:39). Tryphon's offer of the city, its troops and its officials sounds like the reward of a loyal ally, so Jonathan comes with only a thousand men.

p: Jonathan's men believe he has been killed, but in fact Tryphon keeps him alive as a hostage.
b: The verb apolōlen means "he has perished". The rumor was false, or at least early: Tryphon holds Jonathan as a prisoner (13:12) and uses him to bargain with Simon (13:15–19), and kills him only later at Baskama (13:23). The narrator reports what the soldiers heard, and the mourning of 12:52 may be the mourning for the men killed at Ptolemais.

a: wipe out their memory from among men
p: The Gentiles' boast echoes Psalm 83:4 and the old threats against Israel.
b: The nations around them hope to make Israel's name vanish, as the enemies in Psalm 83:4 say: "Come, we will wipe them out so they are no nation; / Israel's name will not be called to mind again". The book tells the story so that the threat fails: Simon rises at once (13:1–9), and the book ends with a memorial on Mount Zion (14:26) and Simon's family tomb "to this day" (13:30).

a: for the laws and the sanctuary
p: Simon names the two things the family fought for: the law of Moses and the Temple.
b: From Mattathias' cry ("Let everyone who is zealous for the law... follow me", 2:27) to the decree for Simon ("so that their sanctuary and the law might stand", 14:29), the book names the same two causes. The plural "laws" includes all the commands Antiochus had banned: circumcision, the Sabbath, the food laws and the Temple sacrifices (1:44–50). The Hasmoneans' claim to rule rests on having saved them.

p: Simon's words recall Elijah's at Horeb, and they are true: of Mattathias's five sons, he is the last.
b: Mattathias had five sons: John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar and Jonathan (2:2–5). Eleazar was crushed under a war elephant (6:43–46), Judas fell in battle (9:18), John was murdered by the Jambrites (9:36–38), and now Jonathan is a prisoner. Elijah had twice said, "I alone am left" (1 Kings 19:10, 14), but God answered that he had kept seven thousand. Simon's speech turns the lament into resolve: the last brother will not spare himself.

a: for I am no better than my brothers
p: Elijah said "I am not any better than my fathers" as he asked to die; Simon says it as he goes to fight.
b: Elijah under the broom bush said, "I am not any better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4), meaning he should die like them. Simon uses the same kind of phrase in the opposite spirit: he is ready to die like his brothers, but he means to live and fight. The book's readers would hear in it the family's whole history of self-giving (2:50, "give your lives for the covenant of our fathers").

a: You are our leader in place of Judas and your brother Jonathan
p: The people acclaim Simon as leader by shout, before any king confirms him.
b: The book stresses that Simon's power comes from the people and from need: they choose him by acclamation here, and the great assembly of 140 BC confirms it in writing (14:35, 41). Jonathan too had been chosen by the people after Judas fell (9:28–31). Only afterwards does a Seleucid king recognize Simon (13:36; 14:38). For a family that was not of the high-priestly line of Zadok, this popular choice was an important part of its claim.

p: Another Jonathan: a commander whose brother Mattathias had stood firm with Jonathan at Hazor.
b: This is not the high priest. "Mattathias son of Absalom" was one of the two officers who did not flee at Hazor (11:70), so the two were probably brothers. Joppa had already been garrisoned (12:33–34); now its non-Jewish inhabitants are expelled. Sinaiticus has a curious slip in 11:70, "son of the psalm-singer" (tou psalmōdou) for "son of Absalom".

p: Tryphon claims Jonathan owes the royal treasury for his posts, a plausible lie in a world where offices were bought.
b: The Greek di' has eichen chreias means "because of the offices (or duties) he held". Seleucid officials paid for their posts and collected taxes for the king; Jonathan had promised payments in return for favors (11:28). A claim of unpaid dues was therefore believable. Simon sees through it (13:17), but he cannot risk the charge that he let his brother die to save money (13:18).
orig: δι᾽ ἃς εἶχεν χρείας (di' has eichen chreias)

a: Still, he sent the money and the boys
p: Simon knew it was a trick and paid anyway. The book defends him; some readers suspect it is answering critics.
b: The narrator explains the payment: if Simon had refused, the people would have blamed him for Jonathan's death (13:18). Some historians, noting how carefully the book defends Simon here, think it answers a charge that Simon did not do enough to save his brother, or that he gained from his death. Josephus tells the story the same way (Antiquities, book 13). The Venetus manuscript (V) reads the opposite, "Simon did not know", which removes the problem but is not likely to be original.

p: Tryphon circles south through Idumea, to come at Jerusalem from the south.
b: Adora is Adoraim (2 Chronicles 11:9), modern Dura, west of Hebron, then in Idumean territory. Blocked by Simon at Adida on the western road, Tryphon swings south to reach Jerusalem from behind, and Simon's army shadows him. The Citadel's garrison begs him to come through the wilderness with food (13:21), but snow stops him (13:22).

a: there was a very heavy snow
p: Heavy snow is rare in Judea but not unknown; it fell on the hills that winter and saved Jerusalem.
b: Snow falls on the Judean hills in some winters (2 Samuel 23:20 mentions a snowy day; Psalm 147:16). A snowstorm would block the steep roads up from the wilderness, and Tryphon's cavalry could not pass. The book does not call it a miracle, in keeping with its plain style, but a reader who remembered the hailstones of Joshua 10:11 could see the hand of Heaven in it.

p: Tryphon kills Jonathan at Baskama in Gilead, east of the Jordan, about 143 BC.
b: The site of Baskama is not known for certain; it lay in Gilead, east of the Jordan, on Tryphon's road back north. Jonathan had led the Jews for about eighteen years, from 160 BC (9:28–31), and had been high priest since 152 BC (10:21). His career is the book's model of diplomacy: he rose by playing the Seleucid rivals against each other, and fell by trusting one of them.

a: took the bones of his brother Jonathan
p: Like Joseph's bones, and Saul's and Jonathan's, the bones are carried home to the family tomb.
b: Burial with one's ancestors mattered deeply. Joseph's bones were carried out of Egypt (Genesis 50:25; Joshua 24:32), and David brought the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from Jabesh to the tomb of Saul's father Kish (2 Samuel 21:12–14). Another Jonathan, another brother's care: the book's readers would hear the parallel. Modein, the family's home town, is where Mattathias was buried (2:70) and where Judas lies (9:19).

p: Six are named; the seventh was probably for Simon himself.
b: The pyramids honor Mattathias, his wife and four sons: John, Judas, Eleazar and Jonathan. Seven were built, so the seventh was most likely meant for Simon. Pyramid-topped tombs were a Hellenistic fashion in the region; the so-called Tomb of Zechariah in the Kidron valley has a pyramid roof. Josephus describes the Modein monument as standing in his own day (Antiquities 13.211–212). The family that had fought Greek ways built itself a Greek-style monument, a point modern historians often make.

a: to be seen by all who sail the sea
p: Modein lies some twenty miles from the coast, so the claim may be pride, or a tall monument on a ridge.
b: Modein (near modern Modi'in) is in the foothills, about twenty miles (thirty kilometers) from the sea. A tall monument on a high point could perhaps be seen from far out on a clear day, but the phrase may also be boastful. The carved ships are striking: they celebrate the new sea power that came with Joppa (14:5). The suits of armor are trophies, of a kind Greek victors set up.

a: It is there to this day
p: The writer speaks from a later time, when the tomb has stood for some years.
b: "To this day" is a phrase of the histories of the Hebrew Bible (Joshua 4:9; 1 Samuel 5:5; 2 Kings 17:41), and it shows the writer looking back. Taken with 16:23–24, it fits a writer working well after Simon's death in 134 BC, late in John Hyrcanus's reign or soon after it (he died in 104 BC).

p: Tryphon has the boy king killed, about 142 BC, and takes the crown himself.
b: Ancient writers say Tryphon had the boy murdered, according to Livy by surgeons who claimed he was dying of an illness (Livy, Summaries 55). Dates differ: coins suggest Tryphon ruled as king from 142 BC. His coins call him Autokratōr, "absolute ruler".

p: The Greek ἄφεσις, "release", here means freedom from tribute: Simon asks Demetrius to cancel Judea's taxes.
b: Aphesis is the Septuagint's word for the year of release (Leviticus 25:10; Deuteronomy 15:1–2) and the New Testament's for forgiveness (Luke 4:18; Acts 2:38). In Seleucid documents it is the legal term for remission of tax. Simon now backs Demetrius II, Tryphon's rival, since Tryphon has murdered Jonathan and only "plunders". The price of his support is the end of tribute (13:37–41).

p: A Hellenistic court title of honor, here written in the plural.
b: "Friend" (philos) was a court rank in the Hellenistic kingdoms, given to high officials and favored allies (10:65; 11:57). The plural, "Friend of Kings", is unusual; it may mean that Simon had been honored by several kings, or simply be a courtesy title. Demetrius addresses Simon as high priest, though he had not appointed him; he accepts what has happened.

p: Simon sent a gold crown and a palm branch (in gold), the usual gifts of loyalty to a king.
b: A gold crown was the customary gift of a subject city or ally at a king's accession, and "crown tax" (13:39) grew out of it. The bain (from an Egyptian word for palm) was probably a palm branch made of gold, as in 2 Maccabees 14:4, where Alcimus brings Demetrius I "a gold crown and a palm". The Vulgate keeps the word (bahem), and the Douay has "the palm" (Douay 13:37). The KJV's "scarlet robe" is a different reading (see the variant).

p: Demetrius cancels the crown tax and all other tolls in Jerusalem, the end of Judea's tribute.
b: Seleucid kings had taken a tribute, a third of the grain, half of the fruit of the trees, a salt tax and the "crown tax" (10:29–30; 11:34–35). Earlier kings had promised to cancel these but kept changing their minds. By forgiving the crown tax and every other toll and pardoning past "errors" (meaning the Jews' backing of Tryphon), Demetrius gives up the claim to tribute. For the book this is the moment of independence (13:41).

a: the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel
p: For the book, 142 BC is the year Israel became free. The image of the yoke comes from the Law and the Prophets.
b: The year 170 of the Seleucid era is 143/142 BC. Ever since Nebuchadnezzar, Judah had paid tribute to Babylon, Persia, the Ptolemies and the Seleucids. Now the burden is gone. The yoke was Scripture's picture for foreign rule and for its end: "I broke the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright" (Leviticus 26:13); Isaiah promised that the oppressor's yoke would be taken off Israel's neck (Isaiah 10:27). The book does not say God did it, but its words invite the reader to see the old promise kept. "Gentiles" translates ethnē, "the nations", meaning the non-Jewish peoples.
orig: ἤρθη ὁ ζυγὸς τῶν ἐθνῶν (ērthē ho zygos tōn ethnōn)

p: 1 Maccabees counts years from 312/311 BC, the start of Seleucus I's rule. The year 170 is 143/142 BC.
b: The Seleucid era began in autumn 312 BC by the Macedonian count, or spring 311 BC by the Babylonian count, which 1 Maccabees seems to use for events in Judea. So the year 170 runs from spring 142 BC (or autumn 143 BC). Dating by a foreign king's era was itself a sign of subjection, which is why the next verse matters: the people begin to count years by Simon instead.

a: In the first year of Simon
p: Contracts began to be dated by Simon's years, as by a king's.
b: Dating documents by a ruler's years was a mark of sovereignty. The rabbis remembered a time when the Hasmoneans had contracts dated "In year so-and-so of Yohanan, high priest of God Most High", and said the sages abolished it because God's name was then thrown away with old bills (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b). On coins, and why none of Simon is known, see 15:6.

a: great high priest, general and leader of the Jews
p: High priest for worship, general for war, leader for government: three offices in one man.
b: Simon is called archiereus megas ("great high priest"), stratēgos ("general") and hēgoumenos ("leader"). The decree of 14:41–47 confirms and defines all three and adds "ethnarch" (14:47). In Israel's history the offices had usually been held by different men, as with Joshua and Eleazar (Numbers 27:21), or Zerubbabel and Joshua (Zechariah 4:14), though Zechariah 6:11–13 and the figure of Melchizedek point the other way. Here they meet in one person, and later Jewish critics objected (see 14:41).
orig: ἀρχιερέως μεγάλου καὶ στρατηγοῦ καὶ ἡγουμένου (archiereōs megalou kai stratēgou kai hēgoumenou)

p: The Greek ἑλέπολις, "city-taker", was a tall movable tower on wheels.
b: The helepolis was made famous by Demetrius Poliorcetes at the siege of Rhodes (305 BC): a tower many stories high, armored, rolled up to the wall, with soldiers who could leap onto it (13:44). That Simon had one shows how far the Jewish army had come since Judas's bands of farmers. Codex Alexandrinus lacks the siege tower here, and in 13:44 has "those in the city"; Swete's text supplies it from Sinaiticus and Venetus (see the variant).

a: to give them terms of peace
p: The Greek says they begged Simon "to give them right hands": the pledge of a truce.
b: Giving the right hand (dexias didonai) was the Greek and Persian gesture of a binding promise, and in war it meant granting terms of surrender. The phrase recurs in 1 Maccabees (6:58; 11:50, 62, 66; 13:50). Paul uses the same words when James, Peter and John "gave the right hand of fellowship" (Galatians 2:9).

a: cleansed the houses where the idols were
p: Simon expels the Gentile citizens and purifies the city, as Judas had purified the Temple.
b: The same verb, katharizō, is used for Judas cleansing the Temple (4:36, 41–43) and for Simon cleansing the Citadel (13:50). Expelling the population and settling "men who keep the law" (13:48) turns a Gentile city into a Jewish one. Modern readers are troubled by this, and the book does not question it. It follows the commands of Deuteronomy 7:5 and 12:2–3 to destroy idols in the land, applied to cities the book counts as part of Israel's inheritance (15:33–34).

a: built a house there for himself
p: Simon makes the city his own base and later stations his son John there.
b: Simon builds himself a residence in the captured city and later makes it the headquarters of John, his commander (13:53; 16:1, 19–21). If the city is Gazara (Gezer), as most scholars think (see the variant at 13:43), excavations there early in the 1900s found a stone with a Greek curse scratched on it, wishing that fire would overtake "Simon's palace". Many take it as a protest from someone forced to work on Simon's building, though its reading and date are debated.

a: On the twenty-third day of the second month, in the year 171
p: The fall of the Citadel, in spring 141 BC, became a yearly festival, remembered in the Scroll of Fasts.
b: The second month is Iyyar (April–May). The year 171 makes the date late spring of 141 BC. Simon declares the day a festival (13:52), like the Day of Nicanor (7:49) and Hanukkah (4:59). Megillat Ta'anit, a list of days on which fasting was forbidden (first century AD), records for 23 Iyyar that the men of the Citadel went out of Jerusalem. The music and palm branches recall the feast of Hanukkah (2 Maccabees 10:7) and the Feast of Booths.

a: with lyres and cymbals and harps
p: The instruments are those David's Levites played: Simon's entry is a Temple celebration.
b: Kinyra (lyre), kymbala (cymbals) and nabla (harps) are the Septuagint's words for the Levites' instruments (1 Chronicles 13:8; 15:16; 2 Chronicles 5:12), and the hymns and songs are Temple praise. The same set greeted the cleansing of the Temple (4:54).

p: Simon's son John, later known as John Hyrcanus, ruled after him from 134 to 104 BC.
b: John is called Hyrcanus by Josephus (Antiquities 13.229–300), but 1 Maccabees never uses the name. Its origin is uncertain. He became high priest and ruler after Simon's murder (16:21–24) and ruled for thirty years. He conquered Idumea, Samaria and parts of Transjordan, destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, and broke with the Pharisees. The book closes with him (16:23–24), which suggests it was written for his house.

a: went into Media to get help
p: Demetrius II marched east against the Parthians, hoping to win troops for his war with Tryphon.
b: The year 172 is 141/140 BC by the Macedonian count used for Seleucid court events (140/139 BC by the Jewish spring count; see 13:41). The Parthians, an Iranian people led by Mithridates I, had taken Media and Babylonia from the Seleucids. Demetrius hoped that the Greek cities of the east would rise to join him. He was defeated and captured about 139/138 BC. The Parthian king kept him in honorable captivity, gave him his daughter in marriage, and let him go home only ten years later (Josephus, Antiquities 13.184–186; Appian, Syrian Wars 67–68).

a: Arsaces, king of Persia and Media
p: "Arsaces" was the throne name of every Parthian king; this one is Mithridates I.
b: Every king of Parthia took the name Arsaces after the founder of the dynasty, so the Greek sources call them all "Arsaces". This one is Mithridates I (about 165–132 BC), who made Parthia an empire. 1 Maccabees calls him king "of Persia and Media", the old names for the Iranian lands, just as Daniel spoke of "the Medes and the Persians" (Daniel 5:28). Rome writes to him too (15:22).

a: The land was quiet all Simon's days
p: The poem of 14:4–15 praises Simon in the words of Judges, Kings and the Prophets.
b: Verses 4–15 are a poem of praise in the style of Hebrew poetry, with short parallel lines. It opens like the refrains of Judges, "The land was quiet for forty years" (Judges 3:11; Judges 5:31; Judges 8:28), the rest that came under a good judge. It ends with the Temple and the law (14:14–15). In between it gathers promises from the Law and the Prophets, so that Simon's peace reads like the age of blessing they described (see 14:12).

a: made an entry to the islands of the sea
p: The coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean: Joppa gave Judea a door to the wider world.
b: In the Hebrew Bible "the islands" or "coastlands" (iyyim) are the far shores of the Mediterranean, the edge of the known world (Isaiah 42:4; Isaiah 66:19; Genesis 10:5). The Septuagint renders the word nēsoi, "islands", as here. Simon's port opens trade with them, and the poem hints that the nations' far coasts now hear of Israel.
orig: ταῖς νήσοις τῆς θαλάσσης (tais nēsois tēs thalassēs)

p: The line takes up the covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:4 and Zechariah 8:12.
b: God promised Israel, if it kept his commands: "The land will give its crops, and the trees of the field will give their fruit" (Leviticus 26:4), and Zechariah repeats the promise for the returned exiles (Zechariah 8:12). The poem does not quote, but it uses the same words in the Greek (hē gē edidou ta genēmata autēs), so that Simon's reign reads as the covenant blessing come true. Leviticus goes on, "I will give peace in the land... with no one to frighten you" (Leviticus 26:6), which 14:11–12 echo.

a: The elders sat in the town squares
p: An echo of Zechariah 8:4: old men and women sitting again in Jerusalem's squares.
b: Zechariah promised: "Old men and old women will again sit in the open squares of Jerusalem, each with a staff in hand because of great age" (Zechariah 8:4, in fresh translation), with boys and girls playing in the streets (Zechariah 8:5). The poem's elders talking "about good things" in the squares and its young men in splendid armor give the same picture of a city at peace, old and young safe.

p: The Greek says the young men "put on glories": fine clothes, or the glory of victory.
b: The plural doxas ("glories") is unusual. It may mean splendid clothes, paired with "the clothes of war" (armor), or, as some suggest, it may reflect a Hebrew phrase like "put on majesty" (Psalm 93:1; Psalm 104:1). Sinaiticus has the singular. Either way the young men are no longer hiding in caves (1:53; 2:31).

a: Each one sat under his vine and his fig tree
t: Under the vine and fig tree
p: Micah 4:4's promise comes true in Simon's days. Does the book present him as fulfilling prophecy?
b: The line takes the words of Micah 4:4: "They will sit, each under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one will make them afraid" (in fresh translation; compare Zechariah 3:10), a promise for "the last days" when the nations stream to Zion (Micah 4:1). It also recalls Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:25). How far does the poem go? Jonathan Goldstein argued that the author meant his readers to see the prophecies fulfilled in the Hasmoneans, so that no further deliverer was needed. Others note that the book never says "fulfilled" and never calls Simon a messiah, and that the decree of 14:41 expects a prophet still to come. Christian readers take Micah 4 of Christ's kingdom, so for them Simon's peace was at most a passing picture. The Psalms of Solomon, written soon after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, accuse the Hasmonean kings of seizing the throne promised to David (Psalms of Solomon 17:4–8), the opposite verdict.

p: The kings who fought the Jews were broken: the Seleucid rivals destroyed one another.
b: In those years Demetrius II was captured (14:3) and Tryphon was soon defeated (15:10–14, 37). "Their kings" means the kings of the enemies who fought Israel. The verb syntribō, "crush, shatter", is the one used of the "great enemy" in 13:51. Sinaiticus and Venetus lack "their".

p: The verb can mean studying the law or enforcing it; the next line, on removing lawless men, suggests enforcement.
b: Exezētēsen ton nomon may mean that Simon studied the law closely, as Ezra "had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law" (Ezra 7:10), or that he made sure it was kept, as in 2:46–48. The poem pairs it with care for "the humble" (tapeinoi, the poor) and the removal of "every lawless and wicked man", which probably means the Jews who had sided with the Seleucids. 1 Maccabees calls them "renegades" and "lawless men" throughout.

a: added many vessels to the sanctuary
p: Antiochus IV had stripped the Temple of its vessels; Simon replaces them.
b: In 169 BC Antiochus IV carried off the gold altar, the lampstand, the table and the cups and bowls (1:21–23). Judas made new holy vessels (4:49). The poem ends with Simon adding more, so it closes where the trouble began: at the Temple. Like Solomon and Hezekiah, a good ruler in Israel's histories cares for the house of God (1 Kings 7:48–51; 2 Chronicles 29:18–19).

a: It was heard in Rome, and as far away as Sparta
p: Chapters 14 and 15 seem to tell the embassy to Rome out of order; scholars still argue how.
b: Numenius is sent to Rome with a gold shield in 14:24, comes back with Rome's letter in 15:15, and in 14:40 the Roman reception is already known at the decree of 140 BC. Most historians think the book has grouped its documents by subject rather than by date. Some think 14:16–24 and 15:15–24 describe one embassy (about 140–139 BC); others think there were two. Rome is unlikely to have written on its own initiative because of Jonathan's death, as 14:16–18 suggests; it normally answered envoys.

p: Rome engraved treaties on bronze, and the decree for Simon copies the custom (14:27, 48).
b: The Romans kept their treaties on bronze tablets on the Capitol, and 8:22 says the treaty with Judas was sent to Jerusalem written on bronze. The Jews follow the same custom for Simon's decree (14:26–27, 48). Bronze meant that the words were public and lasting, unlike papyrus or leather.

a: The rulers and the city of the Spartans
p: The letter's opening, "the rulers and the city", fits the Spartan state of the time, which had no king.
b: By the 100s BC Sparta was ruled by magistrates, the ephors, not by kings; "the rulers and the city" suits that. The reply is a typical Greek decree: it records what the envoys said and orders a copy to be kept in the public archive. For that reason many historians who doubt the letter of Areus (12:20–23) think this one may be genuine, or close to a genuine document.

t: A shield of half a ton?
p: A thousand minas of gold would weigh about half a metric ton. The figure probably gives the shield's value.
b: A mina weighed about a pound (roughly 0.45–0.6 kg), so a thousand minas would be some 450–600 kg of gold, far too heavy to carry as a shield. Most commentators take it as the value of the gift rather than its weight, or as an exaggeration. Gold shields were standard gifts to Rome from friendly kings and cities. In Rome's letter the shield is worth five thousand minas in Alexandrinus but one thousand in Sinaiticus and Venetus (see the variant at 15:18).

a: So they established freedom for Israel
p: The Greek says "they established freedom for him", meaning for Israel, or possibly for Simon.
b: The words estēsan autō eleutherian are "they established freedom for him (or it)". "Him" is most likely Israel, named just before, so the Plain says "for Israel". Some read it as "for Simon", meaning that the people confirmed his deeds of liberation, which leads into the decree. The KJV ends its verse 26 at "confirmed their liberty" and begins 27 with the bronze tablets; the Greek sets them in verse 26. The verse division differs, not the text.

a: on a pillar on Mount Zion
p: In 1 Maccabees "Mount Zion" is the Temple mount, not the hill that bears the name today.
b: 1 Maccabees uses "Mount Zion" for the Temple and its hill (4:37, 60; 5:54; 7:33). The modern "Mount Zion" southwest of the Old City got its name later. Setting the decree up there put the Temple's authority behind Simon. 14:48 says the tablets stood in the enclosure of the sanctuary.

a: On the eighteenth of Elul, in the year 172
p: The decree was passed on 18 Elul 172, in September 140 BC, the third year of Simon.
b: Elul is the sixth month (August–September), just before the new year of Tishri. The year 172 of the Seleucid era, counted from spring 311 BC, runs from spring 140 to spring 139 BC, so the date is September 140 BC. Simon's first year was 170 (13:41–42), so 172 is his third. Elul is named in the Hebrew Bible only at Nehemiah 6:15, when the wall was finished, an apt echo for a decree about walls and freedom.

t: Saramel: a place or a title?
p: No place called Saramel is known. It may be a Hebrew phrase left untranslated.
b: Alexandrinus reads en Saramel; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the Vulgate have "Asaramel". No such place is known. Scholars have proposed that the Greek translator kept a Hebrew phrase: ḥatsar 'am El, "the court of God's people" (the Temple court where the assembly met), or sar 'am El, "prince of God's people", a title of Simon, so that the original read "in the third year of Simon, high priest and prince of God's people". Neither has been proved. The Plain keeps the name as it stands.

p: The Hasmoneans belonged to the priestly course of Jehoiarib, the first of David's twenty-four courses.
b: Joarib is Jehoiarib, whose lot came out first when David divided the priests into twenty-four courses (1 Chronicles 24:7); Mattathias is introduced as a priest of that family (2:1). So the family was priestly, and of the first rank, but not of the high-priestly house of Zadok, which had held the office for centuries until the crisis of the 170s BC. That is one reason the people's decree (14:41) matters so much: it gives the office to a new family by public consent. Sinaiticus and Venetus add "priest" here.

a: he was gathered to his people
p: The old biblical phrase for death, used of Abraham, Moses and Aaron.
b: The Greek prosetethē pros ton laon autou is the Septuagint's rendering of the formula for the death of the patriarchs: Abraham "was gathered to his people" (Genesis 25:8), and so Isaac, Jacob, Aaron and Moses (Genesis 35:29; Genesis 49:33; Numbers 20:24; Deuteronomy 32:50). The decree honors Jonathan in the language of Israel's founders.
orig: προσετέθη πρὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ (prosetethē pros ton laon autou)

a: He spent much of his own money
t: A ruler who pays his soldiers
p: Like a Greek benefactor, Simon pays for the army from his own wealth.
b: Greek cities honored benefactors who spent their own money on the city, and decrees like this one list their gifts. The decree for Simon is written in that style: Simon armed the soldiers and paid their wages (opsōnia, the word Paul uses in Romans 6:23, "the wages of sin"). It also shows a change: the Jewish army is now a paid, standing force.

p: The Greek πίστις here is faithfulness, loyalty to the nation, not religious faith.
b: Pistis means trust, faithfulness or loyalty. The decree says the people saw Simon's pistis and the justice and pistis he kept toward his nation. The same root returns in 14:41 (a "faithful prophet") and 14:48 (a "secure" place). A ruler's faithfulness to his people was a common theme of Greek honorary decrees. The KJV and the Vulgate read differently here (see the variant).
orig: τὴν πίστιν τοῦ Σίμωνος (tēn pistin tou Simōnos)

a: who had made themselves a citadel
p: The decree places the Citadel in "the City of David", the old city south of the Temple.
b: 1 Maccabees says the Seleucids fortified "the City of David" as their Citadel (1:33). In the Hebrew Bible the City of David is the ridge south of the Temple mount that David took from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:7–9). That is the main evidence for placing the Citadel there; Josephus puts it in the "lower city" (Antiquities 12.252). See the note at 12:36.

a: King Demetrius confirmed him in the high priesthood
p: The decree reaches back to Demetrius's letter of 142 BC (13:36–40); by now Demetrius was in Parthian hands.
b: Demetrius had addressed Simon as high priest in 142 BC (13:36), and the decree recalls it. By September 140 BC Demetrius may already have marched east (14:1–3). The decree counts royal recognition as one ground of Simon's office, beside his deeds and the people's choice; but it lists the king's act after the people's (14:35), which shows where the real authority now lay.

p: Simon's office is "forever", until God speaks again through a prophet. The clause assumes prophecy had ceased.
b: Twice before, the book has said that no prophet was there: the stones of the defiled altar were stored until a prophet should come to say what to do with them (4:46), and the distress after Judas's death was the worst since prophets had ceased to appear (9:27). The people act for now; a true prophet may later decide otherwise. Readings. (1) Many scholars see here the belief, stated later by Josephus (Against Apion 1.41) and the rabbis (Tosefta Sotah 13:3), that prophecy ended with Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. (2) Others think the clause also met objections to a non-Zadokite high priest by leaving room for God's own verdict. (3) Christian readers link the expected prophet with the "prophet like me" of Deuteronomy 18:15, a hope still alive in Jesus' day (John 1:21; John 6:14), and with Christ (Acts 3:22). Whether this statement that prophets were no longer seen rules the book out as Scripture is carded on the book's opening page.
orig: ἕως τοῦ ἀναστῆναι προφήτην πιστόν (heōs tou anastēnai prophētēn piston)

p: The decree makes the high priesthood and the rule hereditary in Simon's family. Not every Jew accepted it.
b: "Forever" (eis ton aiōna) means a hereditary office, passing to Simon's sons (14:49; 16:3). The words recall the promise to Phinehas, "a covenant of priesthood for all time" (Numbers 25:13), which Mattathias had already invoked (2:26, 54), and the oath of Psalm 110:4, "You are a priest forever." Augustus's decree calls Hyrcanus II "high priest of God Most High" (Josephus, Antiquities 16.163), and the rabbis remembered contracts dated by "Yohanan, high priest of God Most High" (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b): the title of Melchizedek, priest and king (Genesis 14:18). Opposition. The Pharisees later asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood (Josephus, Antiquities 13.288–292). The Psalms of Solomon denounce the Hasmoneans for seizing David's throne (17:4–8). The Qumran scrolls' "Wicked Priest" is often identified with Jonathan or Simon (see the hasmoneans topic). The question "What power may rulers have over the church?" is carded at 2 Chronicles 26.

a: that he should take charge of the sanctuary
p: "That he should take charge of the sanctuary" appears in both 14:42 and 14:43, probably a copyist's repetition.
b: The phrase hopōs melē autō peri tōn hagiōn stands twice, at the start of the list in 14:42 and again in 14:43. Such a repeat is usually a slip, a scribe's eye returning to the same words. The KJV moves the second one to the end of its verse 42 ("that, I say, he should take charge of the sanctuary"). The Plain keeps both, as the manuscripts do. The clauses "by his authority men should be put in charge" are compressed in Greek, and their sense is that Simon appoints the officials.
orig: ὅπως μέλῃ αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν ἁγίων (hopōs melē autō peri tōn hagiōn)

a: clothed in purple and wear gold
p: Purple and gold were the marks of a king; Simon alone may wear them.
b: Seleucid kings sent purple robes and gold clasps to men they honored: Alexander Balas sent them to Jonathan (10:20, 62, 89; 11:58). The decree reserves them for Simon (14:44). He is not called king; the Hasmoneans took that title only with Aristobulus I (104–103 BC) or Alexander Jannaeus, according to Josephus (Antiquities 13.301) and Strabo (16.2.40). But in dress, in dated contracts and in power, Simon is a king in all but name.

a: call a gathering in the country without him
p: The decree forbids anyone to gather an assembly without Simon's leave, a guard against rivals.
b: The ban on calling a systrophē (a gathering, or a plot) without him protected the new order against both the old high-priestly families and the Hellenizers. The penalty clause (14:45) makes the decree a binding law. Sinaiticus and Venetus read "it shall not be lawful" in the future, and "turn back" for "gather"; the sense is the same.

p: "Ethnarch", ruler of a nation, is a title below king. Rome later gave it to Hyrcanus II and Archelaus.
b: Ethnarchēs means "ruler of a people". It named the head of a nation that governed itself under a greater power. Antiochus VII uses it of Simon (15:1–2). Later Rome gave the title to Hyrcanus II (47 BC) and to Herod's son Archelaus (4 BC; Josephus, Jewish War 2.93), and Paul speaks of King Aretas's ethnarch in Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32).

a: copies of it be placed in the treasury
p: A copy of the decree was stored in the Temple treasury, where Simon's family could produce it.
b: Greek cities kept honorary decrees in public archives, and the Temple treasury (gazophylakion, the word of Mark 12:41 and John 8:20) served Jerusalem that way. The point was legal: Simon "and his sons" could prove their rights. The author of 1 Maccabees seems to have used such archives, which is one reason historians value his documents.

p: Antiochus VII, younger son of Demetrius I and brother of the captured Demetrius II, comes to claim the throne.
b: Antiochus VII was raised at Side in Pamphylia, so he was called Sidetes. When his brother Demetrius II was captured by the Parthians (14:3), he sailed from "the islands" (probably Rhodes), married his brother's wife Cleopatra Thea, and won the kingdom from Tryphon (15:10–14). He was the last strong Seleucid king. After Simon's death he besieged Jerusalem and forced John Hyrcanus to pay tribute again (Josephus, Antiquities 13.236–248), which 1 Maccabees does not tell. He died fighting the Parthians in 129 BC.

p: The Greek λοιμοί, literally "plagues", was a common insult: pests.
b: Loimos means "plague, pestilence", and Greek used it for a person who was a public nuisance. The KJV has "pestilent men". The word comes back in Rome's letter (15:21) for the Jews' own renegades. In Acts 24:5 Paul's accusers call him "a plague" (loimos).

p: The Greek ἀφαιρέματα usually means portions set apart as offerings; here it most likely means tax remissions.
b: In the Septuagint an aphairema is a portion "taken off" for God, a contribution or offering (Exodus 29:27–28). In this royal letter, beside "any other exemptions" in the same verse, it most likely means amounts taken off the taxes, exemptions. The KJV's "oblations" follows the usual biblical sense. Sinaiticus and Venetus use the plainer aphemata ("remissions") and "gifts".

p: Antiochus allows Simon to mint coins, but no coins of Simon have been found.
b: The right to mint was a sign of sovereignty. Bronze coins once credited to Simon, with the words "for the redemption of Zion", are now dated to the revolt against Rome in AD 66–70. The earliest Hasmonean coins bear the name of a high priest Yehohanan (John Hyrcanus I or II) or of Alexander Jannaeus. Either Simon never used the grant, or he had no time: Antiochus soon broke his promises (15:27).

a: Jerusalem and the sanctuary are to be free
p: Seleucid kings granted favored cities the status of "free", or "holy and inviolable".
b: Kings granted cities with famous temples the title "holy and inviolable" and freedom from royal garrisons and taxes. Demetrius I had offered Jerusalem the same (10:31). Freedom for the city and the Temple meant no Seleucid official over them. The Citadel, which had been the symbol of royal power, had already fallen (13:49–52).

p: The year 174 is 139/138 BC. The army deserts Tryphon for the Seleucid heir.
b: Antiochus VII landed at Seleucia in Syria in 138 BC. The troops went over to him because he was of the old royal line and Tryphon was a usurper who had killed a child king. Tryphon fled south to Dor (15:11).

p: An old harbor town on the coast south of Mount Carmel, mentioned in Joshua and Kings.
b: Dor (Greek Dōra) was a Canaanite city (Joshua 11:2; Joshua 17:11), the seat of one of Solomon's district officers (1 Kings 4:11), and a fortified port in Hellenistic times. Its walls held out for a while; Tryphon escaped by sea to Orthosia (15:37). Excavations at Tel Dor have found Hellenistic fortifications and lead sling bullets, one of them inscribed "For the victory of Tryphon" and dated 138/137 BC (Dov Gera, Israel Exploration Journal 35, 1985), evidence of this very siege.

p: Either Lucius Caecilius Metellus (consul 142 BC) or the consul Calpurnius Piso of 139 BC.
b: Rome had two consuls each year. No consul called Lucius fits the date of Simon's embassy exactly. The candidates are Lucius Caecilius Metellus Calvus, consul in 142 BC, or, with a slip in the first name, the consul Calpurnius Piso of 139 BC, whom many prefer for an embassy of 139. The letter is addressed to King Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, and copies go to the others (15:22–23). Its form, a consul writing for the Senate to allied kings, fits Roman practice, and most scholars accept it as based on a real document, though Josephus gives a similar decree under a later Hyrcanus (Antiquities 14.145–148), and the two are sometimes thought to be the same.

a: hand them over to Simon the high priest
p: Rome asks its allies to hand Jewish fugitives back to Simon, to be judged by Jewish law.
b: The clause gives the high priest authority over Jews outside Judea, at least over those who had fled from his rule, probably the Hellenizers of the Citadel. Centuries later Saul of Tarsus carried "letters from the high priest" to the synagogues of Damascus to bring followers of Jesus back to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1–2; Acts 22:5; Acts 26:12). Historians debate whether the high priest really had such a power in Paul's day; this letter is the nearest precedent.

a: to Attalus, to Ariarathes and to Arsaces
p: Demetrius II of Syria, Attalus II of Pergamum, Ariarathes V of Cappadocia and Mithridates I of Parthia.
b: Attalus II ruled Pergamum (159–138 BC), Ariarathes V Cappadocia (about 163–130 BC), and "Arsaces" is the Parthian king (14:2). Rome still writes to Demetrius II as king of Syria, perhaps because the letter dates from before news of his capture, or because Rome had not recognized Antiochus VII. The list is a map of Rome's eastern world in the 130s BC.

p: Many of these places had Jewish communities, and several appear in Acts.
b: The list runs through Greek cities and islands (Delos, Samos, Cos, Rhodes, Cnidus), regions of Asia Minor (Caria, Pamphylia, Lycia), Crete (Gortyna), Cyprus and Cyrene in Libya. Jews lived in many of them, and the letter shows Rome's concern for them as "friends". Pentecost brought pilgrims "from Pamphylia" and "the parts of Libya near Cyrene" (Acts 2:10); Paul sailed past Cos and Rhodes (Acts 21:1) and preached at Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13:13; Acts 14:24–25). Sampsames is uncertain; many think it is Amisus (Samsun) on the Black Sea.

p: The Greek ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ, "on the second", may mean the second day, or a second time.
b: En tē deutera has no noun. The KJV reads "the second day". Some think the narrative picks up after the Roman letters with "a second time" (Antiochus camped against Dor a second time), and a corrector of Sinaiticus added "day" (hēmera). The Plain follows the KJV's reading, which is the simplest.

p: Once Antiochus has the upper hand, he cancels his promises to Simon.
b: The pattern runs through the book: Seleucid kings promise much when they need Jewish help and take it back when they are strong (Demetrius II, 11:53; compare Tryphon, 12:45–48). The book's readers learn not to trust them, while still dealing with them. Antiochus's grant of 15:2–9 lasted only months.

a: his sideboard with gold and silver dishes
p: Athenobius is amazed at the wealth of Simon's court, a sign that Judea is now a power.
b: The kylikion was a sideboard where cups were displayed at a banquet. Like the Queen of Sheba at Solomon's court (1 Kings 10:4–5), the king's Friend is overwhelmed by what he sees. The narrator is proud of the splendor; other Jewish writers would later blame the Hasmoneans for living like Greek kings.

a: We hold the inheritance of our ancestors
p: Simon answers like Jephthah: the land is Israel's by right, taken back from those who seized it.
b: Jephthah made a similar argument to the king of Ammon: Israel had not taken another people's land, and "whatever the LORD our God has driven out from before us, we will take possession of" (Judges 11:15, 24). Simon claims the whole land as an ancestral inheritance (klēronomia, the Septuagint's word for the land given to the tribes, Numbers 26:53–56). Historically, Joppa had never been Israelite, and Gezer became Israel's only under Solomon (1 Kings 9:16); Antiochus's claim was the legal one by Seleucid law. The two arguments, from Scripture and from treaty, talk past each other.
orig: τῆς κληρονομίας τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν (tēs klēronomias tōn paterōn hēmōn)

a: For them we will give a hundred talents
p: Simon offers a tenth of the thousand talents demanded, as payment for Joppa and Gazara, not as tribute.
b: Antiochus asked for five hundred talents for the towns and five hundred for damages and taxes (15:31). Simon offers a hundred, not as tribute, which would admit the king's rule, but as a price for two towns that had "done great harm". Athenobius takes it as an insult and does not answer.

p: Tryphon escapes north by sea to Orthosia, near Tripoli in Lebanon. 1 Maccabees does not tell his end.
b: Orthosia was a port north of Tripoli. Other ancient writers say that Antiochus pursued Tryphon to Apamea, where Tryphon died, perhaps by his own hand, about 138 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.224; Strabo 14.5.2). 1 Maccabees drops him here, its interest now on Simon's war with Antiochus's general.

p: The king's governor of the coast fortifies Kedron, near Jamnia, to raid Judea.
b: Cendebeus is known only from this story and from Josephus's retelling. Kedron is probably modern Qatra, near Gedera, between Jamnia (Yavneh) and the Judean hills; the Vulgate has "Gedor" (Vulgate 15:39). From there his cavalry could raid the roads of the Shephelah. The threat brings John into the story as commander (16:1).

a: from our youth to this day
p: Like Mattathias on his deathbed (2:49–70), Simon passes the fight to his sons.
b: The scene matches Mattathias's farewell, where the father charges his sons to be zealous for the law and names Judas commander (2:49–70). Simon is old (16:3), and he gives the war to Judas and John. The words "things went well in our hands" (euodōthē) repeat the decree's praise (14:36). Unlike Mattathias, Simon does not die in bed: the next scene is his murder.

p: The Greek says only "in the mercy"; God's mercy is meant, but the book avoids naming God.
b: En tō eleei leaves the giver unnamed, in the book's reserved way of speaking of God (see 12:15). The KJV supplies "by God's mercy". The prayer that ends the verse, "may the help from Heaven be with you", is the same reserved language.

p: The text does not say whether Simon or John chose the army and led it across the stream.
b: The subject of "He chose" (16:4) and of "he crossed first" (16:6) is not named. Simon has just handed the command to his sons (16:3), and John leads the pursuit (16:9), so most readers take John as the leader. Modein, Simon's home town, is where the army camps.

p: Like Judas before him (5:43), the leader goes first into the water and the frightened army follows.
b: Judas crossed a stream first at Raphon (5:40–43), and Joshua's priests stepped into the Jordan before the people (Joshua 3:13–17). A general who leads from the front was the ideal of the book, and it fits the family's heroes. Here the stream separates the armies, and crossing it was the dangerous step.

a: put the cavalry in the middle of the infantry
p: For the first time the book shows a Jewish army with cavalry, set among the infantry against a stronger enemy horse.
b: Judas's army had no cavalry; it fought on foot against Seleucid horse (4:1, 28–31). By John's time the Jews have horsemen (16:4). Placing them among the foot soldiers protected them against the enemy's larger cavalry. The detail shows a state army, raised "from the country" (16:4) and paid (14:32).

p: The trumpets echo the law of Numbers 10:9; some manuscripts call them "holy" trumpets.
b: Numbers 10:9 commands: "When you go out to battle in your own land against an enemy who is attacking you, sound the battle blast on the trumpets. Then the LORD your God will remember you, and you will be rescued from your enemies." Judas's men blew trumpets before battle (3:54; 4:13, 40; 5:33). The Venetus manuscript and the Latin call them "holy" trumpets, the priests' silver trumpets (see the variant).

p: The Greek "it" is feminine; it may be Azotus or Kedron.
b: Enepyrisen autēn, "he burned her", needs a feminine noun. Azotus (Ashdod), named just before, is the likeliest: Jonathan had burned it once before with its temple of Dagon (10:84). Some think it means Kedron (16:9), whose name is also feminine in Greek. The Vulgate makes it the towers ("he burned them"). Sinaiticus and Venetus say two thousand men fell (see the variant).

p: Simon's son-in-law, governor of the rich Jericho plain, plots to rule the country himself.
b: Nothing else is known of Ptolemy or his father Abubus, whose name may be Semitic (perhaps Habub). He had a Greek name, a royal appointment as governor (stratēgos) of the Jericho plain, with its balsam and date groves, and wealth enough to buy the army's officers (16:19). Being the high priest's son-in-law (16:12) gave him a claim of his own. He looked to Antiochus VII for support (16:18).

p: Pride goes before the fall, as with Uzziah and the kings of Babylon.
b: "His heart was lifted up" (hypsōthē hē kardia autou) is the Septuagint's phrase for the pride that leads to ruin: Uzziah's heart was lifted up to his destruction (2 Chronicles 26:16), and Hezekiah's (2 Chronicles 32:25). Alexander's pride opened the book ("his heart swelled with pride", 1:3), and Antiochus IV entered the sanctuary "in his arrogance" (1:21). The book ends as it began, with a proud man.
orig: ὑψώθη ἡ καρδία αὐτοῦ (hypsōthē hē kardia autou)

a: in the year 177, in the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat
p: Simon dies in Shebat 177, early in 134 BC. He had ruled for eight years.
b: Shebat is the eleventh month (January–February), named in the Hebrew Bible only at Zechariah 1:7. The year 177 gives February 134 BC. Simon had led the nation since 143/142 BC. Like Samuel, who went around Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah judging Israel (1 Samuel 7:16), he is touring the towns when he dies.

p: A small fortress above Jericho; the name survives at the spring of Ain Duk.
b: Josephus calls the place Dagon and says it lay above Jericho (Antiquities 13.230; Jewish War 1.56). The name Dok survives in Ain Duk, a spring northwest of Jericho, and the fortress is usually placed on the cliff above it, Jebel Quruntul (the traditional Mount of Temptation). The Greek says Ptolemy received them "with deceit" (meta dolou), the same word used of Tryphon's trap for Jonathan (13:17, 31).

a: When Simon and his sons were drunk
p: Simon is killed at a feast, like Amnon and King Elah. Josephus tells the aftermath differently.
b: Killing a guest at a drinking party breaks the most basic law of hospitality. The Bible tells of Absalom having Amnon killed "when Amnon's heart is feeling good with the wine" (2 Samuel 13:28), and of Zimri killing King Elah while Elah was "drinking himself drunk" (1 Kings 16:9–10). Josephus says that Ptolemy killed Simon but took his wife and two sons prisoner; John Hyrcanus besieged the fortress, Ptolemy tortured the mother on the walls, and at last killed her and the sons and fled (Antiquities 13.228–235; Jewish War 1.54–60). 1 Maccabees says the sons died with their father.

p: The narrator's verdict uses the words of Genesis 44:4 and Psalm 35:12.
b: Joseph's steward was told to ask, "Why have you paid back evil for good?" (Genesis 44:4), and the psalmist complains, "They pay me back evil for good" (Psalm 35:12). Ptolemy owed everything to Simon, his father-in-law, which makes the murder worse. The book gives it no more comment.

p: John is stunned, but he moves first and kills the assassins sent for him.
b: The Greek exestē sphodra means he was "beside himself", the same verb used of Athenobius's amazement (15:32). John's quick action saves the dynasty. The book ends its story here, without telling the siege of Dok or Antiochus VII's siege of Jerusalem, which Josephus reports (Antiquities 13.229–248).

p: The book ends with the formula that closes each king's reign in Kings and Chronicles.
b: Kings ends each reign: "The rest of Solomon's story, all he did and his wisdom, is written in the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds, is it not?" (1 Kings 11:41; compare 1 Kings 14:29). The Septuagint of Kings has idou tauta gegraptai, "look, these are written", the words used here (16:24). The author presents John Hyrcanus as a king in the line of Israel's kings and his book as the next volume of Israel's history. Judas's story ends the same way (9:22).

a: the book of the days of his high priesthood
p: The reference to John's annals dates the book to the end of his rule or after his death in 104 BC.
b: "The book of the days" renders the Hebrew divre hayyamim, "annals", the Hebrew name of Chronicles. A writer who can point to the annals of John's whole high priesthood, "from the time he became high priest", seems to write when that rule was over, or nearly so. Many therefore date 1 Maccabees around 100 BC, late in John's reign (134–104 BC) or early in that of Alexander Jannaeus; some put it earlier. It must be before Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, since Rome is still a friend. Josephus follows 1 Maccabees closely to about 13:42 and then tells Simon's rule from other sources; some scholars took this to mean his copy lacked chapters 14–16, but most think he simply changed sources.
orig: ἐπὶ βιβλίου ἡμερῶν ἀρχιερωσύνης αὐτοῦ (epi bibliou hēmerōn archierōsynēs autou)
